note: Man-of-war’s men: sailors who serve on a warship rather than a merchant ship.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Man-of-war”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Liberty: leave granted to sailors to go ashore for a short time.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Liberty”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: like Aldebaran among the lesser lights
note: Aldebaran is a bright star in the constellation Taurus, known since Greek times. Melville compares the sailor to it among the dimmer stars around.

anchor: That signal object was the “Handsome Sailor”
note: A phrase for the finest-looking sailor, admired by his shipmates as a natural leader.
Vainglorious: boastful and full of empty pride, showing off.
Regality: the dignity of a king.

anchor: native African of the unadulterate blood of Ham
note: In Genesis, Ham is a son of Noah, and nineteenth-century writers wrongly treated him as the ancestor of Africans. Melville uses that old and racist phrase for a Black sailor.
source: The Bible (King James Version), Genesis 9:18, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

anchor: the displayed ebony of his chest
note: Ebony: a very dark black wood. Melville uses it as a color word for the sailor’s skin.
Pagod: an idol, or the temple that houses one. Melville compares the sailor to a statue.
Joachim Murat was a French cavalry general under Napoleon, famous for his showy costumes. A nautical Murat means a sailor who dressed up elaborately.
A nickname for a bragging, swaggering boatman of the American canals.
Vaporing: bragging. Groggeries: low drinking places that sold grog.
The Handsome Sailor is also a champion fighter among sailors.
Reefing: tying up part of a sail to shrink it. Close-reefing shrinks it as far as possible.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Reef”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: The yard is the spar that holds a sail; the yard-arm is its end. Weather means the windward side.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Yard-arm”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: The Flemish horse is a short footrope hung under a yard’s end for sailors to stand on.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Flemish horse”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Bucephalus was the favorite horse of Alexander the Great, a famous war-horse of ancient times.

anchor: tossed up as by the horns of Taurus
note: Taurus is the Bull, a constellation and sign of the zodiac. Melville pictures the sailor tossed upward by a bull’s horns against the sky.

anchor: cheerily hallooing to the strenuous file along the spar
note: Strenuous: energetic, hard-working. File: a line of men.
Comeliness: pleasing good looks. The sailor’s looks and strength go together.
Cynosure: a person who attracts everyone’s attention. The word first meant the North Star.
Welkin: an old word for the sky. Billy’s eyes are sky-blue.

anchor: a foretopman of the British fleet
note: Foretop-men are stationed in the fore-top, a platform on the foremast, to set and take in sail.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Foretop-men”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: having been impressed on the Narrow Seas
note: Impressment was the British navy’s practice of forcing men into service, especially sailors. The Narrow Seas are the English Channel and the nearby waters.
A seventy-four was a warship with seventy-four guns. Outward-bound means leaving home waters for a distant station.
H.M.S. stands for His Majesty’s Ship. Indomitable means impossible to defeat, an ironic name for this ship.

anchor: short of her proper complement of men
note: Complement: the full number of crew a ship needs.

anchor: in the gangway the boarding officer
note: The gangway is the opening in a ship’s side where people come aboard.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Gangway”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Pounced: swooped down suddenly, as a hawk does.
Mustered: gathered for inspection. The quarter-deck is the rear upper deck, reserved for officers.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Quarter-deck”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: some scruples in view of the merchantman
note: Scruples: moral doubts or hesitations that keep a person from acting.
Demur: an objection. Billy does not protest.

anchor: the protest of a goldfinch popped into a cage
note: Melville compares Billy’s easy submission to a bird that is caught and caged without a struggle.
Acquiescence: quiet acceptance without resistance.

anchor: a ploughman of the troubled waters
note: A merchant captain is called a ploughman of the sea, working the waves as a farmer works a field.
Corpulence: being fat or heavily built, a polite word.
Prepossessing: making a good first impression.
The forecastle is the forward part of a ship where the crew lives.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Forecastle”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: The spirit-locker is a locked cupboard in the captain’s cabin where liquor is kept.
A joke on the officer’s habit of drinking. He waters the dryness of duty with liquor.

anchor: a fertilizing decoction of strong waters
note: Decoction: a liquid made by boiling. Strong waters: spirits.
Alacrity: quick, cheerful willingness. He plays the host with forced cheer.
Irrepressible: unable to be held back.
Grog: rum diluted with water, the sailors’ ration in the Royal Navy.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Grog”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Rueful: full of regret, sorrowful.

anchor: my forecastle was a rat-pit of quarrels
note: A rat-pit was an arena where rats were set against dogs. He means the crew always fought.

anchor: like a Catholic priest striking peace in an Irish shindy
note: Shindy: a noisy quarrel. The captain compares Billy to a priest stopping a brawl.

anchor: a virtue went out of him
note: Echoes the Gospels, where Jesus feels “virtue” go out of him when a woman touches his clothes. Billy’s effect on others is like a gift flowing out.
source: The Bible (King James Version), Luke 8:46, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

note: A figure of speech: he sweetened the ill-tempered men.
Treacle: molasses, a thick sweet syrup. The captain says the crew flocked to Billy as insects do to syrup.
Buffer: here, a rough fellow who takes the knocks for the others.
A game-cock is a fighting rooster, bred to be bold.
Must needs: has to. Bestir: stir himself into action.
Dog-watch: one of two short watches of two hours between 4 and 8 in the evening on a ship.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Dog-watch”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: the lubber was astonished at the celerity
note: Lubber: a clumsy or inexperienced sailor. Celerity: speed.
The capstan is a vertical drum on a ship’s deck that is turned to haul in cables.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Capstan”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: From the Sermon on the Mount: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.”
source: The Bible (King James Version), Matthew 5:9, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

anchor: his hard tack is not sought for by sailors
note: Hard tack: hard ship’s biscuit, the basic food of the navy.
Privily: privately, in secret. Some captains secretly resent losing their men.
Apollo was the Greek god of beauty, music, and the sun. The Lieutenant jokes that Billy looks like a god carrying a suitcase.

anchor: Boot and saddle for the cavalryman
note: Boot and saddle: a cavalry bugle call ordering the troops to mount.

anchor: bag and hammock for the man-of-war’s man
note: Sailors in the navy kept their things in a bag and slept in hammocks.

anchor: The hard-headed Dundee owner was a staunch admirer of Thomas Paine
note: Thomas Paine wrote The Rights of Man (1791) in answer to Edmund Burke’s attack on the French Revolution. Dundee is a Scottish port city.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Paine, Thomas”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Paine%2C_Thomas; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Dundee”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Dundee

anchor: Burke’s arraignment of the French Revolution
note: Edmund Burke’s Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) condemned the Revolution. Paine’s book was a reply.
Stephen Girard was a wealthy Philadelphia merchant and banker whose ships were mostly named for French writers such as Voltaire.
Denis Diderot was a French philosopher of the 1700s, a leading writer of the Enlightenment.
The coxswain is the man in charge of a small boat and its crew.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Coxswain”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: The taffrail is the rail around a ship’s stern.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Taffrail”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: a terrible breach of naval decorum
note: Breach: a breaking of a rule. Decorum: proper behavior.
Impressment: forced naval service. The Lieutenant suspects Billy’s farewell is a sly joke about it.

anchor: by no means of a satirical turn
note: Satirical: mocking, using irony to ridicule. Billy has no such streak.
Fatalist: one who accepts that events are fixed by fate.
An able-seaman is a fully skilled sailor, above the ordinary seaman in rank and pay.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Able”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Sailors worked in two watches, port and starboard. The fore-top is the platform on the foremast.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Watch”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: not at all disliked for his unpretentious good looks
note: Unpretentious: modest, without showing off. His looks are plain and natural.
Happy-go-lucky: cheerfully carefree, taking life as it comes.

anchor: saddish mood which in some partook of sullenness
note: Sullenness: gloomy silence, resentful bad mood.
Kith and kin: friends and family.
